items.title: HackerTube: YouTube built from videos recommended by HN
items.content:
It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with: hackertube.org !

Opus downloaded all comments of HackerNews, filtered them down, ran Sonnet over them in a workflow, got rid of spam and low grade content, and narrowed them down to just 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila!

This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5 <3.

items.title: An outsider's perspective on Scion and Mononoke
items.content:
An outsider’s perspective on Scion and Mononoke

Recently, Anthropic wrote a blog post about their new centralized version control system Scion . As someone working on the Source Control team at Databricks, where we have a huge monorepo and are exploring different options, I figured it might be useful to share my perspective here.

(Obligatory disclaimer: This post represents my own views, not my employer’s.)

I recommend reading Anthropic’s post before continuing to read this one.

You may also want to pre-read Rain Paharia’s Anthropic’s Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke and the follow-up More on Anthropic’s Scion ripping off Mononoke .

Before we get into the weeds, it might be helpful to you to know where I’m coming from.

If you’re not interested in this, you can jump to the Technical Commentary section.

I have never worked at Facebook, but one of my all-time favorite tech talks is Durham Goode’s Scaling Mercurial at Facebook from Git Merge 2017. Goode was the longest-serving and most senior member on Facebook’s Source Control team. ( source )

The talk covers various interesting aspects for both the server side and the client side. For the server side, some of the topics include solving push contention with server-side rebasing (pushrebase), using scalable object storage for commits, moving various source control queries to the server, etc. For the client, there’s mention of the smartlog and other CLI commands for easier manipulation of history (compared to rebasing in Git).

However, more so than the technical aspects of the talk (which are interesting in their own right!), the main thing that has stayed with me throughout these years is the deep care for users that is reflected in Goode’s tone and words. It’s a bit difficult to convey this without the power of voice, You should watch the presentation!

but here are some quotes which reflect this:

In the context of hg smartlog : hg smartlog gives you a focused view of your branches and how they relate to the development trunk.

I know Git can produce this kind of UI if you know the incantation, but the critical thing here is not that it can be done; it’s that it becomes the default view of their source-control environment. That is where the power comes from: making it really intuitive for users to use source control and understand the concepts without reading a man page.

In the context of hg absorb : hg absorb auto-magically identifies the right commits in a stack to squash fixes into and rewrites history accordingly. This makes it easier to work with stacked changes.

This is the type of UI that we need to be inventing for our users: ones that match their intent and do it to the best of their ability, without making the user understand everything they have to do. It’s a little bit magic, but it’s magic in a very clean way. I think a lot of user experiences could benefit from this approach.

If you want to undo an amend or undo parts of a commit in Mercurial, you just run unamend and uncommit. You don’t have to understand a reflog; you don’t have to get a PhD to understand reset anymore. It just works, and it gives users confidence that they can recover from mistakes. That’s one of the most important things we can do: provide user experiences that give them confidence in what they’re doing.

On the user experience side, we as a source control community need to do a better job of building UIs that are accessible, intuitive, and that enable novice users to be power users. Everything I just talked about is how we are trying to do that for our users at Facebook. If the Git community could do that, the massive number of Git users taking advantage of it has the potential to redefine productivity for an entire generation of users.

Over the years, the possibility of these workflows lingered in my mind as I continued working with Git. I tried building my own wrappers on top of the git CLI to do some of these things, but I couldn’t get the performance to be reasonable…

items.title: At A Worker-Run Game Studio, Employees Voted To Lose Their Jobs
items.content:
In early September, Montreal game studio KO-OP announced it would be “saying goodbye” to 13 people, citing–like so many others–difficulty finding funding. But unlike other layoffs in the games industry, which tend to strike suddenly from on-high, those affected had been involved in the decision from the beginning, and had actively voted for the outcome.

“As with all our company's operational decisions, this one was made democratically,” KO-OP wrote in its announcement. “Our members are regularly updated on our cash flow situation, and were made aware of this upcoming shortfall well in advance. Membership then appointed a group to plan for this eventuality, and ratified their recommendations. Team leads and our elected executives will also be impacted by these reductions. We believe this level of transparency and accountability ought to be a minimum requirement for all organizations.”

— KO_OP: 🪐 Wishlist Young Suns on Steam! ( @ko-op.com ) September 10, 2026 at 11:32 AM

It’s an unusual process for any company, but not necessarily one for KO-OP : The studio–which was founded in 2012, and has made games including Gnog, Goodbye Volcano High, and its current project Young Suns –operates as a co-operative. Everyone at the studio, which was roughly 30 people prior to the cuts, makes the same amount of money, $90K CAD ($63K USD). In addition to members’ game development work, they’re required to help with administrative tasks by joining committees dedicated to topics like hiring and finance, and membership meets every other month to talk as a group about how things are going and to vote on proposals about the studio.

“We try to call ourselves ‘worker run,’ because all of our operations are democratically operated and managed,” co-founder and studio director Saleem Dabbous told Aftermath over a video call, noting that the studio is still working toward legally becoming a co-op.

As the studio has grown, especially during production of Young Suns , its structure and operations have had to grow with it. Prior to the cuts, membership had elected a six-person “executive committee,” and it was this committee that was tasked with coming up with proposals for how to deal with KO-OP’s financial problems and, ultimately, who to let go.

Dabbous and former narrative designer Jenna Yow, who lost their job, largely referred to the cuts as furloughs, since KO-OP hopes to hire affected workers back. Affected workers are still eligible to receive any profits from Young Suns , and they can still attend studio meetings and vote on company decisions. They “still have the ability and the choice to be involved with the operations of the co-op at large, because it's in their best interest to see how things are progressing in case we're able to rehire them,” said Dabbous.

“With [a] layoff, generally, it's like a handshake, like a goodbye, it's done… Our intent is essentially to try to do the best we can by everybody, within our means, and to try to keep that as transparent as possible.”

And while workers didn’t know ahead of time who would be affected, they knew the cuts were coming and had time to prepare. This proved valuable for Yow, who was hired four and half years ago to work on narrative for Goodbye Volcano High as their first full-time job in the games industry out of college. During the furlough discussions, they had been trying to move to KO-OP’s Montreal office from the Seattle area. Aware they might not have a job and subsequently a visa if they moved, they were able to instead plan a move to live near family on the East Coast.

“Really the biggest benefit of it [was] just having the time to prepare… and then just kind of make plans accordingly, which is not something a lot of other people at other studios get to do,” Yow told Aftermath in the video call.

“Even though this situation is not one I would wish on anybody, I do feel like it's probably the best way it could have happened for anyone.”

items.title: The lost malloc()
items.content:
(Sorry, I couldn't resist not putting a catchy title :)

Prompted by another project idea that popped into my mind, I did some Unix archaeology and looked at the original sources . This is the most fun I've ever had reading someone else's code - probably due to the historical significance. But also because of how delightfully approachable it was, compared to modern monstrocities.

This is a short(-ish) post regarding how they handled the mundane and boring task of allocating and managing memory (in C). In the future I'd like to read more about Unix the OS, its design, architecture & implementation.

In a PDP far, far away, our journey begins with the fourth edition of Unix, released November '73, more than half a century ago . C actually first appeared in the second edition, released the year before, but wasn't extensively used. V4 is special because even the majority of the kernel was written in (let's call it "medieval") C by that point. The system had grown, however, and it was quite capable. You'll find that many Unix things we have today in POSIX-land were already present in V4.

Super fun fact: A tape containing V4 was only found last year ! Previously, it was thought to be completely lost to time.

While cleaning a storage room, our staff found this tape containing UNIX v4 from Bell Labs, circa 1973

The first interesting bit is found among the C "compiler" sources. In quotes, because it wasn't a monolithic compiler as we know it today. Rather, it was a set of distinct tools which you chained in order to get an object file from C code.

In /usr/c/c20.c:814 , from what I can gather a very primitive optimiser, if you will (referred to as "C object code improver" in V5; there aren't many comments in V4) you see:

Isn't that fascinating? This routine is used throughout the program to allocate memory. And if you squint, this is just a linear allocator. It aligns the size, checks if the region is big enough, otherwise tries to extend it. On failure, it just cold-exits. Which means callers don't have to check for NULL every single time, and indeed they do not.

The "region" isn't named, unlike how you'd do it today with arenas. However, the above does have a nice property, in that by using sbrk() , when we extend the heap, no pointer is invalidated.

And they don't bother freeing memory, because why would they? There's no need. Everything exists for the lifetime of the program.

This is the most interesting bit in my opinion, and the reason why I chose that title.

In Dennis' directory, you find a file named malloc.c . And you see two functions there:

Seems familiar? Yep, it's mfree() with an m . These functions obviously deal with memory (de)allocation, and are the precursor to the ones we're familiar with today. But , the interfaces are different.

malloc() receives an additional first argument called mp (for "map"), and so does mfree() . What is that? Well, let's see how they're used:

So, they pass in some objects coremap and swapmap . What are those?

They're just flat memory regions! So these malloc() and mfree() work on explicit memory regions ! Not only that, mfree() receives the size of the object it is deallocating, as it should . Those are just infinitely-times better interfaces than traditional malloc() / free() .

Imagine using a library that has such an interface. You could deallocate all its memory resources by just discarding the entire region you delegated to it. Heap corruption bugs would be less severe because you could partition memory. You could trivially limit the amount of memory third party code allocates. The list goes on and on...

(Side note: They slightly messed up here and the regions should've been sized CMAPSIZ/2 and SMAPSIZ/2 respectively. They did fix that later.)

However, I don't think all these benefits were in the minds of Dennis and Ken. So why did they go with that interface and why did they partition memory to "core" and "swap"? The reason is, I believe, just hardware constraints.…
items.title_ko: '잃어버린 malloc()': 초기 Unix의 메모리 관리 방식 살펴보기
items.summary_ko: 작성자가 1973년 11월 출시된 Unix 4판(V4)의 원본 소스를 직접 읽으며 초기 Unix의 메모리 할당과 관리 방식을 살펴본 글이다. V4는 커널 대부분이 C로 작성되었고, 오늘날 POSIX 계열에 있는 여러 기능이 이미 갖춰져 있었다. 작성자는 원본 소스를 읽으며 큰 재미를 느꼈다고 밝힌다.
items.content_ko: 작성자는 Unix 4판(V4)의 원본 소스를 살펴보는 '유닉스 고고학' 작업을 하며, 다른 사람의 코드를 읽은 것 중 가장 재미있었다고 말한다. C 언어는 2판에서 처음 등장했지만 널리 쓰이지는 않았고, V4에 이르러서는 커널의 대부분이 C로 작성되어 있었다. 시스템은 이미 상당히 성장해 있었고, 오늘날 POSIX 계열에서 익숙한 많은 기능이 V4에 이미 존재했다. V4가 담긴 테이프는 작년에 발견되었다고 한다. 글의 주된 내용은 평범하지만 중요한 작업인 C에서의 메모리 할당과 관리를 Unix가 어떻게 처리했는지이며, 작성자는 앞으로 Unix 운영체제의 설계와 구조, 구현도 더 읽어보고 싶다고 밝힌다.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다

items.summary: 🚨 CVE-2026-95863 📢 Source: apache 💣 CVSS Score: 7.6 (HIGH) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Improper neutralization of input during web page generation in Apache Wicket. Apache Wicket generates JavaScript
items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-95863 📢 Source: apache 💣 CVSS Score: 7.6 (HIGH) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Improper neutralization of input during web page generation in Apache Wicket. Apache Wicket generates JavaScript that refers to the elements it renders, and writes into that JavaScript two values it derives itself: a component's markup id, and the input name of a form component, which is built from component ids. Both are placed inside single-quoted JavaScript string literals without being escaped for that context, so a value containing a single quote or a backslash ends the literal, and what follows is parsed as script and runs in the application's origin when the page loads. A markup id is the value passed to org.apache.wicket.Component#setMarkupId(String), or the id attribute written in the component's markup, or an id Wicket generates, in that order. The first two are supplied by the application in an HTML context, where both characters are legal and where Wicket escapes them correctly when it writes the same value into the id attribute of the element; a generated id cannot contain either. An input name is derived from the ids of the components between the form and the form component, and a component id was rejected only for ':' and '~'. In org.apache.wicket:wicket-core on 9.x and 10.x, org.apache.wicket.markup.head.OnEventHeaderItem#forMarkupId(String, String, CharSequence) quotes the id it is given into a Wicket.Event.add call, and components in both wicket-core and wicket-extensions reach it through #forComponent(Component, String, CharSequence). On every affected version, org.apache.wicket.markup.html.form.Form writes its markup id and the id of its hidden-fields container into such literals, org.apache.wicket.markup.html.form.FormComponentUpdatingBehavior writes an input name, and org.apache.wicket.markup.html.form.upload.MultiFileUploadField writes two markup ids and an input name. On 8.x, Form also writes an input name into the action of a submitting link, and on 8.x and 9.x Form#appendDefaultButtonField writes an input name into a name attribute with no escaping at all, so a value containing a double quote escapes the attribute into markup. org.apache.wicket:wicket-extensions is affected in its own right and not only through wicket-core: AjaxEditableLabel, AjaxIndicatorAppender, AjaxDisableComponentListener, UploadProgressBar, KittenCaptchaPanel, Palette, FilterForm and, on 9.x and 10.x, TrapFocusBehavior and AjaxListPanel each build their own JavaScript containing a markup id. An application is affected where a markup id or a component id carries one of those characters. Wicket does not put one there itself, so the value comes from the application: an id set on a component, an id attribute in a template, or a component id derived from data. None of those is a JavaScript context from the application's point of view. The Content-Security-Policy that Apache Wicket 9.x and 10.x send by default does not prevent this. The generated script is written into a script element carrying the per-response nonce, so the injected code is part of a script the policy admits. The fixed versions check an id where it enters instead of escaping each place it is written. A component id and a markup id may no longer contain a quote, a backquote, a backslash, braces, angle brackets, a semicolon, an ampersand or a control character, and a markup id may not contain parentheses or square brackets either; a component constructed with such an id, or given such a markup id, fails with an exception. This issue affects Apache Wicket: from 8.0.0 through 8.19.0, from 9.0.0 through 9.24.0, from 10.0.0 through 10.11.0. Users of Apache Wicket 7.x or older, which are no longer supported, should upgrade to a supported version. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 8.20.0, 9.25.0 or 10.12.0, which fix the issue. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-01T22:30:47.259Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-95863

items.title: An Italian farmer found some unknown seeds in his attic and planted them
items.content:
At his farm near Parma, Italy, Claudio Grossi offers a visual history of his miracle grain in photos, crackers and loaves.

Sometime in the early 1990s, Claudio Grossi, a 40-year-old farmer in Parma, in northern Italy, was cleaning his attic when he turned up an old sack full of seeds that he couldn’t identify. The bag, he was sure, had been left by his late great-grandfather, who’d started the farmstead around 1915. Grossi had no idea how long the seeds had been sitting there, deprived of water, soil and sun. Dry and cracked, the kernels looked so old in the palm of his hand that he doubted anything would ever sprout from them. He carried the bag down the stairs, shook the seeds out into a pile of manure and then forgot about them.

To his surprise, the seeds soon sprouted a few different types of wheat. One was particularly striking: At six feet high, its plants were about twice as tall as commercial wheat. But the most remarkable feature came when it developed ears—the grain-studded parts at the top of the plant. All of the wheat types Grossi had previously seen grew only one such ear. But the tall wheat grew a full seven ears, always in the same pattern: a long one with six shorties bunched up around it like little fingers. Even the kernels themselves were bigger than those of average wheat. And unlike the typical pale-yellow wheat kernels, they came in a rainbow of colors—yellow, black, red, white and even green, sometimes all on the same stem. Grossi, a grain farmer his whole life, had never seen anything like it. “I thought it was a freak of nature,” he says. He couldn’t find a mention of it in agricultural books.

Ears grown from the very first seeds Grossi discovered in his attic. Grossi prizes these first grains, now preserved under glass in his kitchen.

For Grossi, a practicing Catholic, the next insight came from a different book altogether. Leafing through a Bible at church one Sunday, he found a passage in the Book of Genesis describing a stalk with seven ears, in a dream that Joseph interprets for the Pharaoh: “And he slept and dreamed the second time: And, behold, seven ears of grain came up upon one stalk, rank and good. And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them. And the seven thin ears devoured the seven rank and full ears.” To Grossi, that sounded just like the mysterious crop in his manure pile.

“I connected the dots,” Grossi says. That grain must be really ancient , he thought. And if people were farming this odd-looking wheat in biblical times, why does no one today?

Back on his farm, Grossi harvested the grain, milled it into flour and baked a loaf of bread in his kitchen. Compared with commercial wheat, the dough didn’t rise well, but as the loaf sat in the oven, it filled the kitchen with a surprisingly nutty and delicious aroma. Once finished, it had a rich, satisfying taste. “You get these notes of sweetness that you can’t find in regular commercial flour,” he says.

Did you know? More miracles of grain in the Bible

In 2 Kings 4:42-44 , Elisha multiplies 20 barley loaves in order to feed 100 men—anticipating Jesus’s “Feeding of the 5,000” in the gospels.

In 1 Kings 17:8-16 , Elisha helps a widow at Zarephath to outlast a drought and famine with only a handful of flour and a little oil.

In Judges 7:9-15 , a Midianite soldier recounts a dream in which a barley loaf tumbles into the camp and overturns a tent. Gideon, the judge and military leader, recognizes the dream as a sign that God will deliver the Midianites into Israel's hands.

In 2 Kings 4:38-41 , during a famine, someone gathers wild gourds and cuts them into a pot of stew. The diners discover that the stew is dangerous and cry out to Elisha. He calls for flour and throws it into the pot—and the stew becomes miraculously safe to eat.

items.title: Pratt parsing is a black box
items.content:
It caught my attention that most of Pratt parsing tutorials that I've stumbled on spend almost all of their time explaining Pratt's algorithm and none explaining the properties behind Pratt that actually matter. Pratt fits into just 9 lines of code if you're programming in a high-level language such as Rhombus:

And here's a secret: that's the least important thing you need to understand about Pratt's. In fact, you don't need to understand this piece at all! Imagine if you were only able to use quicksort if you understood its implementation. Imagine if you were only able to use files if you knew how to implement a filesystem from scratch. It's the same logic here. If you lack the power to abstract, you'll arrive nowhere in computer science because that's how the whole field works. In fact, I wrote the backbone of a heavily Pratt-based parsing machinery for a compiler that I've been writing since last year w/o even bothering to understand the above snippet in any detail.

Not convinced? Think for a second on how they do in traditional parsing techniques: compiler compilers! They use code generators to spit the parsing algorithm because just a minuscule crowd bothers to learn what the parsing engine is actually doing. It's no different with Pratt. However Pratt is so small that you can just copy'n'paste these 9 lines of code in your project and call it a day instead of adding a new complex dependency to your project. The algorithm hasn't changed since 1973 and it's not gonna change now.

In this article I'll go over what you actually need to keep in mind for Pratt parsing. The point won't be about memorizing any of it though. The point is about acquiring a mindset. As long as you acquire the mindset you don't need to even bother to remember even a single word of what I say here.

The only tutorial on Pratt parsing that I can firmly recommend to someone who has never been exposed to the topic is actually a talk that Douglas Crockford gave in the conference GOTO 2013 ¹ . Douglas Crockford nailed it when he stated:

Pratt takes parsing which is a really complicated thing and reduces it to one simple question: What do we expect to see to the left of a token ?

At first glance it may look like a mystical statement devoid of meaning, but that's the question that becomes the framework on how you face parsing problems and it'll rewire your brain to internalize the Pratt parsing mindset. That's the most important thing you need to understand. You register semantic actions for two categories: nuds and leds. A nud is a token that expects nothing to its left (nud stands for null denotation) while a led expects something (led stands for left denotation).

Traditional parsing techniques register semantic actions to production rules. Here's an example I took straight from GNU Bison's manual:

The text between the braces is code that executes when the BNF-like grammar on the left matches. I'm gonna repeat myself because that's really important: traditional parsing techniques register semantic actions to production rules (which by definition are non-terminal symbols). In contrast Pratt parsing registers semantic actions to the terminals themselves instead. That's a fundamental shift on how you face parsing problems.

Here's a stripped down version of the code for the tables that I have in my compiler right now:

rule_c < token :: lbrace , token :: nud :: parse_lbrace > ,

rule_c < token :: code :: less_than_sign , token :: nud :: parse_enter_type_scope > ,

rule_c < token :: code :: plus_sign , token :: nud :: parse_unary_plus > ,

rule_c < token :: code :: minus_sign , token :: nud :: parse_unary_minus > ,

rule_c < token :: code :: dplus_sign , token :: nud :: parse_preincrement > ,

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Lenovo's 'encrypted' fingerprint USB drive is just an unencrypted SD card in a fancy case
items.content:
Security researcher Xusheng Li found that a Lenovo ThinkPlus FU100 fingerprint USB stick, sold as an AES-256-encrypted device for data security, ended up being just a plain SD card internally, HackingPassion reports. The fingerprint reader only enabled the USB connection, and nothing on the card was actually encrypted. An AI-assisted follow-up last week discovered what Li calls backdoor accounts on another maker’s drive, as well as hardcoded keys in other supposedly secure USB storage products.

The FU100 is “just an SD card in a fancy case,” Li said in a March conference talk. It is, as a result, trivial for anyone with physical access to get to the drive’s data. One of his takeaways: “‘Hardware security’ can be pure marketing.” This isn’t the first time drive makers’ own encryption has failed , and it won’t be the last.

The original ThinkPlus FU100 analysis happened last year, with an interim fix using epoxy over the card. A later fix by Lenovo, put out early this year for the FU100, FU200 and TU800 drives, as well as the TSD303 SSD, requires owners to call a China service line, then either send devices back for replacement or get an on-site firmware upgrade. Lenovo advises backing up data first and strongly recommends wiping the drive before sending it in, which is quite an inconvenience. Lenovo rated the advisory’s severity as high, and one of its three CVEs covers the configuration software, which could let a local, logged-in user bypass device authentication and enroll an untrusted fingerprint.

The same research also turned up a different flaw in Lenovo’s TSD303 external SSD. Its data actually was encrypted, but the drive sent the correct password back over USB in plain text for the software to compare, making it easy to capture. The first fix came three months after the initial report, using block cipher encryption with a key derived from a timestamp-like value. Lenovo’s software could derive that key, and the first software fix is vulnerable if taken apart, making it not useful for protecting data if a device is stolen. A later fix, late last year, has the drive check the typed password itself, so the correct one never leaves the drive.

The same software development kit used for the drive covered nine other devices from multiple vendors, most of which could also reveal passwords to a savvy actor. In addition, two left data unencrypted on a microSD card. The full list of vendors was blacked out on Li’s slides.

AI agent use for driving reverse-engineering tools continues to increase. AI has also been exposing more security flaws recently. Li used OpenAI’s Codex, an AI programming-centric tool, with his employer’s reverse-engineering tool against other vendors’ protection schemes. Netac’s tool took about seven minutes to break, as Codex found a fixed key built into the program, along with the user’s password written to diagnostic logs.

Copy protection differs from direct access, as the intent is to allow the recipient to view files, just not make copies of them. KakaSoft’s USB Copy Protection has an internal password the program builds itself, which Codex rebuilt to decrypt a test file without the user’s password in around 26 minutes. Nexcopy’s Copy Secure took about 10 minutes, with its key unlocked by a certificate built into the viewer app. Separately, SecZure’s YutianDun has two hidden “backdoor” accounts with simple passwords, discovered with time-travel debugging, stepping through a timeline trace. However, Li’s comments suggest that malicious intent cannot be assumed.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-87718 📢 Source: apache 💣 CVSS Score: 2.3 (LOW) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Apache Wicket 10.10.0, 10.11.0 and 9.24.0 do not set the Content-Security-Policy headers on a page whose render request handler is wrapped in more than one IRequestHandlerDelegate. The framework unwraps only a single delegate level when deciding whether a request renders a page, so with a deeper chain, for example an application-provided delegating request mapper combined with CryptoMapper, the page is served without any CSP header even though CSP is enabled, and no error or warning is raised. The nonce-based protection Wicket applies to inline scripts and styles, together with any other CSP directives configured by the application, is thereby lost for those pages, exposing them to content injection the policy was meant to prevent. Applications on stock Wicket that do not wrap request handlers themselves are not affected. Versions before 10.10.0 and 9.24.0 handled nested delegates correctly. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 10.12.0 or 9.25.0, which fix the issue. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-01T22:28:35.032Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-87718

items.title: Introducing Kwi, a new KDE terminal emulator
items.content:
Introducing Kwi, a new KDE terminal emulator

I've started work on a new KDE application. It's called Kwi (pronounced kwee ).

Kwi is designed to provide users of KDE Plasma and other free desktops with a modern and fast terminal, built on a robust tech stack and following the latest KDE HIG and UI conventions.

In some sense, the product vision for Kwi is to be kind of unexciting: Just what you want and expect out of a KDE Plasma terminal. Of course, given the powerful nature users generally expect from KDE software, this does not make the project lacking in ambition. :-)

To achieve things, Kwi builds on libghostty-vt from the excellent Ghostty project and familiar, mature KDE Frameworks such as KPty . It has a very speedy GPU-accelerated (Vulkan or OpenGL) renderer powered by the Qt Scene Graph. Its user interface is built with the latest and greatest by Kirigami , making it blend in very well among more recent KDE applications and the Plasma desktop.

In keeping with the theme, Kwi's icon/logo is a cute little terminal ghost. This is also how it came to bear its name: kwisin , or more typically gwisin , is a romanized form of 귀신 - Korean for ghost. It's pronounced a little bit like kwee-shin .

Compared to the venerable and mature Konsole , Kwi is young and new. At the moment it offers a more streamlined feature set than Konsole, carefully realized using KDE's latest HIG patterns. The way forward will be to build on this slowly and carefully, using everything we've learned as a community about running mature design processes over the last decade or so (hello, VDG!). It's a chance to canvass the scene, take stock of how other terminals implement more recent innovations in this space, and compete with a KDE spin on things.

Konsole is very intertwined with the older of the two user interface tech stacks in Qt, QWidget . QWidget typically renders using the CPU, and so does Konsole. Newer KDE software (including Plasma itself) typically uses Qt Quick and benefits from GPU acceleration via Vulkan or OpenGL instead. This is what Kwi does as well. For certain terminal applications the performance gain (3x-35x faster than Konsole depending on what's being benchmarked) can make an actual big difference in the user experience, but generally it should also help reduce battery usage.

Kwi is built on libghostty-vt , a project that describes itself as an ecosystem play - provide a headless lib that takes care of all the gnarly terminal parsing and state, enable downstream projects and become sort of a rising tide that lifts all boats. It's starting to really deliver on this promise lately, outpacing other terminal implementations on support for modern TUI features and not hoarding all this good only for itself. While the library will only make an ABI/API stable v1.0 promise at some point in the next 4-6 months, it's already slowly being adopted by big and popular projects, including Neovim, Ghostel and many more. Here's a list .

Kwi marries the library to the KDE/Qt tech stack, which allows the project to focus mostly on desktop integration and rendering performance, two areas where KDE's software stack is generally second to none. The combination of the two offers some improvements over Konsole already, for example:

General UI lift-up to the latest KDE HIG

3x–35x faster overall performance, depending on the benchmark E.g. 870 fps in DOOM-fire-zig on a test system, vs. 23 fps in Konsole

Rendering GPU-accelerated rendering via Vulkan or OpenGL

Better support for using the KDE Plasma system color scheme, including live changes

Improved support for correct handling of Wayland fractional scaling

Improved terminal text rendering Improved rendering of text decorations (e.g. z-sorting for complex underline styles)

Improved support for ligatures, especially when they interact with coloration and selection

Support for mode-2027 grapheme widths, Nerd Font icon scaling, etc.

Improved support for Powerline and geometry symbols

items.title: Innocent People Are Being Accused of Shoplifting by Faulty AI-Facial Recognition Systems at an Alarming Rate: "It's the stuff of Kafkaesque nightmares."
items.content:
From New York City to the streets of Tokyo , creepy AI-facial recognition security systems are quickly becoming a common sight across the world. Unfortunately for many, the tech is nowhere near ready for the responsibility of live use as the troubling rise of false-positive matches makes clear.

In the United Kingdom, AI surveillance systems in retail stores have led to a surge in customers being wrongly accused of shoplifting. TechRadar highlighted a number of recent cases throughout the country, where shoppers say false accusations have left them shaken, with a feeling that their privacy had been horribly violated.

As one woman identified as Mary told the publication, her husband has been socially “isolated” after a quick jaunt into a Home Bargains store for vitamins went awry. When the stores’ system flagged the anonymous man as a shoplifter, the couple was forced to leave by management, seemingly without any chance to refute the accusation.

“I was scared to go into a shop,” the man told TechRadar .

Another man was said to be “shaking from head to toe” following his wife’s removal from a Budgens chain store for the crime of stealing “loads of meat” days before — an accusation complicated by the fact that they hadn’t set foot in the store for months.

In these and other cases, the publication reports a dizzying labyrinth of corporate bureaucracy and vague insinuations that leave innocent people unable to access their local businesses, and with little recourse to clear their name.

In the UK, individuals can file Subject Access Requests, or SARs, which are like US-Freedom of Information Act requests but for private companies. Though the avenue technically exists for those wrongly accused of shoplifting, it’s a massive undertaking just for the hope of clearing your name — and requires handing over even more private information to private companies.

As head of advocacy at civil liberty group Big Brother Watch Jack Coulson told TechRadar , it’s “the stuff of Kafkaesque nightmares to be trapped in a maze of bureaucracy and forced to hand over even more personal data just to be told the accusation.”

More on facial recognition: Innocent Man Freed After Spending Over 50 Days in Jail Due to Horribly Inaccurate AI Facial Recognition Tech

items.summary_ko: 뉴욕과 도쿄 등지의 매장에 도입되는 AI 얼굴인식 보안 시스템이 잘못된 매칭을 일으키면서, 영국에서는 무고한 손님이 절도범으로 몰리는 사례가 늘고 있다. TechRadar가 보도한 사례에서 Mary의 남편은 Home Bargains에서 비타민을 사던 중 절도범으로 지목되어 매장 측으로부터 퇴장을 요구받았고, 이후 사회적으로 고립된 느낌을 받았다고 한다. 기사는 이 기술이 실시간 운영에 충분히 준비되지 않았다고 지적한다.
items.content_ko: 뉴욕과 도쿄 등에서 AI 얼굴인식 보안 시스템이 빠르게 늘고 있지만, 오탐 사례가 계속 나와 실제 운영 준비가 부족하다는 지적이 나온다. 영국에서는 소매점의 AI 감시 시스템 때문에 무고한 손님이 절도범으로 잘못 지목되는 사례가 급증했다고 TechRadar가 전했다. Mary라는 여성에 따르면, 남편이 비타민을 사러 Home Bargains에 들렀다가 시스템에 절도범으로 표시되었고, 매장 측은 반론할 기회도 거의 주지 않고 부부를 나가게 했다. Mary의 남편은 이 일 이후 주변에서 고립된 느낌을 받았다고 한다. 또 다른 남성은 Budgens 매장에서 며칠 전 '고기를 잔뜩' 훔쳤다는 혐의로 아내가 쫓겨난 뒤, 온몸을 떨 만큼 충격을 받았다고 말했다. 한 남성은 가게에 들어가기가 무서워졌다고 밝혔다. 기사는 이런 상황을 '카프카적 악몽'에 비유한다.

items.title: 'Mother of all editors' Emacs is 50
items.content:
By a startling coincidence, so is its arch-rival Vi

Howler will have AI answer your questions, then burn the chat

LibreOffice's 'no AI' stance meets LLM-assisted code

Matrix takes sovereign messaging into the realm of the tech giants

How Google fumbled the frontend with Angular 2

ZacOS 9 and Mavernix: Two classic Apple desktops find their Wayland to Linux

No lesser authority than the MIT Technology Review says that the Emacs editor has turned 50 years old. But then, it is biased — Emacs was invented in MIT's AI lab.

Simson Garfinkel's article is simply called EMACS turns 50, but the sub-heading explains why it matters more:

"How the MIT AI Lab's text editor gave birth to the free software movement."

There are multiple timelines and accounts of the origins of Emacs, and it is not a single monolithic application. The name is an abbreviation for " E diting MAC ro S ", and the original editor for which this set of macros was developed was TECO – "Text Editor and COrrector," written by Dan Murphy in 1962. Murphy  died earlier this year at the age of 83.

The inimitable Jamie Zawinski has an encyclopedic Emacs Timeline – as he mentions at the start, his interest being that he long ago maintained a fork of GNU Emacs, originally called Lucid Emacs . It's still around, under its later name XEmacs. There are a lot of forks and re-implementations of Emacs out there, and we are not going to go into all of them, or this article would become a book – one only interesting to programmer-archeologists (to use a term coined by the late great Vernor Vinge ).

As for who originally wrote those Editing Macros, though, another history has quotations from several of the people involved: On the Origin of Emacs in 1976 . (Note – some of the quotes still contain the | symbols that marked quoted text.)

This credits Lisp boffin Guy L. Steele  Jr with the original work in 1975, but in it, Steele says:

"RMS is responsible for the names 'E' and 'EMACS'. RMS still deserves 99% or 99.9% or 99.99% or 99.999% of the credit for taking a package of TECO macros and turning it into the most powerful editor on the planet."

RMS is of course Richard Stallman, and the page also quotes some emails from RMS on October 23 and 31, 1976. Mind you, just a few years after the event, in a 1981 talk now preserved on the GNU website, Stallman said, "I began the development of EMACS in 1974 with an improvement to TECO". Like all the best FOSS, even in its very early stages, it was a collaborative effort – but around late October 1976 is when RMS took over the bulk of the development.

Of the many forks of Emacs over its half a century of development, some are still just about hanging on in there. When we looked up the link for XEmacs, we were surprised to see that there was a new release: XEmacs 21.5.37 "lettuce" appeared just last month. And even the forks have forks: in this case, SXEmacs , last updated in 2020.

Most of the changes in XEmacs and SXEmacs eventually made their way back upstream to GNU Emacs, which is still in active development, although as The Register reported in 2008 , RMS is no longer the primary maintainer. GNU Emacs 31.1 appeared in August.

Cards on the metaphorical table: this vulture is not an Emacs user. We have tried. A major influence was one of the Reg FOSS desk's favorite writers, Neal Stephenson, who in 1999 published an essay called In the Beginning… Was the Command Line . (It was later republished as a rather short book, but the text is still online .) In it, he says:

"In the GNU/Linux world there are two major text editing programs: the minimalist vi (known in some implementations as elvis ) and the maximalist emacs . I use emacs, which might be thought of as a thermonuclear word processor. It was created by Richard Stallman; enough said. It is written in Lisp, which is the only computer language that is beautiful. It is colossal, and yet it only edits straight ASCII text files, which is to say, no fonts, no boldface, no…
items.title_ko: '편집기의 어머니' Emacs 탄생 50주년
items.summary_ko: MIT Technology Review가 Emacs 탄생 50주년을 맞아 Simson Garfinkel의 기사 'EMACS turns 50'을 실었다. 기사는 MIT AI 연구소의 텍스트 편집기가 자유 소프트웨어 운동을 낳았다는 점을 짚는다. Emacs는 Dan Murphy가 1962년에 만든 TECO를 원형으로 하는 매크로 집합에서 출발했다고 소개된다.
items.content_ko: MIT Technology Review의 Simson Garfinkel은 Emacs가 50년이 되었다는 기사를 실었고, 부제는 이 편집기가 MIT AI 연구소에서 자유 소프트웨어 운동을 낳았다고 설명한다. Emacs의 기원에 대해서는 여러 기록과 설명이 있으며, Emacs는 단일한 하나의 애플리케이션이 아니다. 이름은 'Editing MACroS'의 줄임말이며, 이 매크로 집합이 개발된 원래의 편집기는 Dan Murphy가 1962년에 만든 TECO(Text Editor and Corrector)다. Murphy는 올해 83세로 세상을 떠났다. 기사는 라이벌 Vi도 같은 해 50년을 맞았다고 전한다. Jamie Zawinski는 Emacs의 역사를 정리한 상세한 타임라인을 작성했다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-111089 📢 Source: apache 💣 CVSS Score: 7.6 (HIGH) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Apache Wicket reads texts from the application's resource bundles — a localized label, a css class name — and writes some of them into the JavaScript and the markup it generates for a component. Those texts are placed inside single-quoted JavaScript string literals and inside quoted attribute values without being escaped for that context, so a text containing a quote ends the literal or the attribute, and what follows is parsed as script or as markup in the application's origin when the page loads. A resource bundle entry is authored for the application and does not say where the framework will write it. The same key is read by the framework into element text, where Wicket escapes it, and into the contexts below, where it did not. A text containing an apostrophe, which is ordinary in several languages, is enough to break the page; a text under the influence of another party is enough to run script. In org.apache.wicket:wicket-core, org.apache.wicket.markup.html.form.upload.MultiFileUploadField writes the org.apache.wicket.mfu.delete message into a JavaScript string literal, and org.apache.wicket.markup.html.form.Form writes the hidden-fields css class into the class attribute of the container it renders for its hidden fields; on 8.0.0 through 8.19.0 and 9.0.0 through 9.24.0 Form#appendDefaultButtonField writes the same css class into a second container. In org.apache.wicket:wicket-extensions, UploadProgressBar writes its UploadProgressBar.starting text into a JavaScript string literal, FilterForm writes the hidden-fields css class into the class attribute of its hidden input markup, and on 9.0.0 through 9.24.0 and 10.0.0 through 10.11.0 TrapFocusBehavior writes its current css class into a JavaScript string literal. The Content-Security-Policy that Apache Wicket 9.x and 10.x send by default does not prevent the JavaScript cases: the generated script is written into a script element carrying the per-response nonce, so the injected code is part of a script the policy admits. It does prevent an inline event handler injected through the attribute cases. This issue affects Apache Wicket: from 8.0.0 through 8.19.0, from 9.0.0 through 9.24.0, from 10.0.0 through 10.11.0. Users of Apache Wicket 7.x or older, which are no longer supported, should upgrade to a supported version. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 8.20.0, 9.25.0 or 10.12.0, which fix the issue. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-01T22:32:09.104Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-111089
items.title_ko: Apache Wicket 리소스 번들 텍스트의 이스케이프 누락으로 스크립트 실행 가능 CVE-2026-111089 (CVSS 7.6, 높음)
items.summary_ko: Apache Wicket이 리소스 번들의 텍스트(현지화된 라벨, CSS 클래스 이름 등)를 JavaScript와 마크업에 이스케이프 없이 넣어 발생하는 취약점(CVE-2026-111089)이다. CVSS 점수는 7.6(높음)이며, 원격 공격이 가능한 것으로 표시되어 있다. 작은따옴표가 포함된 텍스트만으로도 페이지가 깨질 수 있고, 외부 영향을 받는 텍스트라면 페이지에서 스크립트가 실행될 수 있다.
items.content_ko: Apache Wicket은 애플리케이션의 리소스 번들에서 읽은 텍스트를 컴포넌트용 JavaScript와 마크업에 쓴다. 이 텍스트는 해당 컨텍스트에 맞게 이스케이프되지 않은 채 작은따옴표로 감싼 JavaScript 문자열 리터럴이나 따옴표로 감싼 속성 값 안에 들어가, 따옴표가 있으면 문자열이나 속성이 끊어지고 뒤따르는 내용이 페이지에서 스크립트나 마크업으로 해석된다. 리소스 번들 항목은 애플리케이션을 위해 작성되며, 프레임워크가 그 값을 어디에 쓸지는 알려주지 않는다. 같은 키는 요소의 텍스트로 읽힐 때는 이스케이프되지만, 위의 다른 컨텍스트에서는 이스케이프되지 않는다. 여러 언어에서 흔한 아포스트로피가 들어 있는 것만으로도 페이지가 깨질 수 있으며, 외부 영향을 받는 텍스트라면 스크립트 실행으로 이어질 수 있다. wicket-core의 MultiFileUploadField는 org.apache.wicket.mfu.delete 메시지를 JavaScript 문자열 리터럴에 쓰는 것으로 언급되어 있으나, 기사 본문은 여기서 잘려 있다.

items.title: TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 / CVSS 9.8
items.content:
Linux's stable kernels shipped a fix on October 11 and 15, 2026 for CVE-2026-98432 , a use-after-free in the IPv4 TCP handshake that a remote, unauthenticated peer can reach. The kernel's own CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8, Critical . The fixed releases are 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 , and 7.3 , and the bug goes back to Linux 4.4. The upstream fix is a four-line change, but most servers run a distribution's kernel, and as of 5:15 PM CDT, October 31, Ubuntu's tracker still reads "Vulnerable" for its kernel on every release, and Red Hat, which now rates the bug Critical too, lists RHEL 8, 9, and 10 as affected with no fix.

Why it's urgent: the bug sits in code every Linux server runs when it accepts an IPv4 TCP connection, before any application sees the connection. Anthropic, whose researcher reported it, says its Claude model wrote a working proof-of-concept exploit that runs commands as root on "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener," with no credentials. Go programs open those listeners by default, per the Go Security Team. See the timeline .

CVE CVE-2026-98432, "ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period," issued by the Linux kernel CNA

Severity Critical, CVSS 3.1 9.8 ( AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H ), the kernel CNA's score. Red Hat also rates it Critical, CVSS 3.1 9.8, raised from Important (8.1) on October 30. SUSE rates it important, Ubuntu rates it High, and Oracle and Amazon rate it Important with CVSS 3.1 8.1.

Weakness Use-after-free of IPv4 option data during the TCP handshake (the record lists no CWE)

Impact Per the CNA's scoring notes: kernel heap contents disclosed to the remote peer, kernel memory corruption, or a crash. Red Hat's bulletin: a remote, unauthenticated attacker "could exploit a race condition during TCP connection request processing to trigger remote code execution."

Fixed in 7.2.10 and 6.18.56 (Oct 11) · 6.12.113, 6.6.159, 6.1.190, 5.15.223, and 5.10.272 (Oct 15) · 7.3 (Oct 18)

No fix yet Ubuntu (every release) and RHEL 8, 9, and 10, as of 5:15 PM CDT, October 31. AlmaLinux's fixed kernels are still in testing. Upstream branches that reached end-of-life before 5.10 get no fix.

Proof of concept Anthropic says Claude built a remote root exploit for servers with a multipath TCP listener. It hasn't published the exploit.

CVE records Published on cve.org on October 15. NVD lists it as "Received," with no analysis of its own, as of 5:15 PM CDT, October 31.

Credit Reported by Xinyang Ge of Anthropic. Fixed by Eric Dumazet and reviewed by Kuniyuki Iwashima, per the fix commit.

Any Linux kernel from 4.4 on that lacks the fix, whether it serves the network directly or hosts containers: a container runs on the host's kernel, so a new image doesn't change anything. IPv6 connections aren't affected by the main issue; the commit says "IPv6 is not affected by the first issue."

Release line Status on Oct 31, 2026 Fixed in Released

7.3 Mainline 7.3 (from 7.3-rc7) Oct 18, 2026

4.4 – 5.4 End-of-life upstream distro fixes only —

Distribution kernels carry backported fixes under their own version numbers, so check the tracker, not the upstream number. As of 5:15 PM CDT, October 31:

Ubuntu: the tracker lists the linux package as "Vulnerable" on every release. On 26.10, 26.04, 24.04, and 22.04 it adds "work in progress" in 7.3.0-10.10 , 7.0.0-43.43 , 6.8.0-149.149 , and 5.15.0-203.213 ; 20.04, 18.04, and 16.04 show only "Vulnerable." Many cloud and hardware-enablement kernels are listed the same way, and no Ubuntu Security Notice has been published.

Red Hat: rated Critical, CVSS 3.1 9.8, since October 30. RHEL 8, 9, and 10 and OpenShift Container Platform 4 and 5 are listed as affected, with no fix; RHEL 6 and 7 aren't affected ( CVE page ). items.summary_ko: Linux 안정 커널은 10월 11일과 15일 업데이트에서 IPv4 TCP 핸드셰이크의 해제 후 사용 취약점 CVE-2026-98432를 수정했으며, 커널 CNA는 이를 CVSS 9.8(Critical)로 평가했다. 원격의 인증되지 않은 상대방이 이 취약점에 도달할 수 있고, 버그는 Linux 4.4까지 거슬러 올라간다. 그러나 10월 31일 오후 5시 15분(CDT) 기준 Ubuntu 추적기는 모든 릴리스의 커널을 여전히 'Vulnerable'로 표시하고, Red Hat은 RHEL 8, 9, 10이 영향을 받으며 수정안이 없다고 밝혔다.

Go Security Team에 따르면 Go 프로그램은 기본적으로 이러한 리스너를 연다.

items.title: so i guess everyone uses llms to think now
items.content:
in recent times i've been asked a lot the question of "what ai model did you find to use this?", practically for all of the articles on this blog. the answer has always been my brain, i have never used ai for any kind of research i published, ever.

the next question is often why, followed up with "you would be so unstoppable with claude mythos" this article should explain why i don't like using ai for my research, and my general opinions on llms in both development and cybersecurity

it's as simple as i do this for fun, and i don't find giving an ai all the fun at poking at something instead of doing it myself fun. put it another way, i like using my brain

i like coding, i like staring at devtools, binary ninja, or whatever else for hours, i like exploring weird library source code and tracing it with nothing but github code search and a dream, it is fun to me. i don't do anything on this blog for money, i do it for fun, the money part is just a nice side effect

but why don't you just offload the tedious bits to ai?

a lot of the tedious bits are still fun, there's some that aren't, but i also cannot take credit for something an llm did for me, and i am wildly uncomfortable with publishing something an llm did for me on my personal blog as a writeup

this blog is mine, all the work on it is mine, or is shared research with other people that are explicitly credited. i cannot take credit for something an llm did for me, and i also cannot credit an llm properly, as they aren't a person

i truly have tried to use llms before, just to try it out. nothing i was going to publish as research, but i really couldn't and it left me never wanting to use an llm again

i don't know how more people don't experience this, but staring at an llms output be confidently wrong eventually to get there in the process, or looking at the commands its running and see some really stupid things its doing drives me crazy to the point i will just stop it before it answers, i cannot handle something being that confidently wrong (even though it'll probably still get there in the end)

i'm not denying these models are powerful

llms are quite powerful machines, we've seen that as of recent, that's for sure, they are still wildly marketed as being more powerful then they are, but i cannot argue that they are infact not powerful, because they are

if you threw an llm at the linux kernel and told it to find an rce without any other guidance, it probably couldn't. you still need skill and experience to guide an llm at the current state

all of these vulnerabilities that we've been panicking over have been found by skilled researchers using llms, likely at a big firm to give them all the tokens they want. because llms still need guidance and not anyone can just do this, no matter what openai or anthropic try to tell you

ai companies have hooked onto cybersecurity as their marketing strategy and it shows, a good example is php2shell. where three companies:

all collaborated on it and released their own blogposts, all seemingly with different narratives

calif went with the narrative of an ai found these php vulns with the help of a human guiding it, while openai went with the agent uncovered critical vulnerabilties, and wiz went with a middle point, still pretty openai-like

openai talked a lot about how they were helping maintainers patch these issues, and mitigate them faster and for more people. which i'm sure they did to an extent, but i don't think they did all they could

they could easily backport these security fixes to older versions of php with the help of ai if they wanted to, it's not like they don't have the compute, they do, they have a lot of it, they're openai

this has been a common trend in the recent days of ai-based cybersecurity where researchers and otherwise companies, drop poc videos of unpatched 0days on twitter, for some reason

this is so clearly marketing, and it does nothing but make everything worse in terms of security. these poc…
items.title_ko: 그래서 이제는 다들 LLM으로 생각하나 보다
items.summary_ko: 작성자는 블로그 글의 리서치에 AI 모델을 사용한 적이 없다고 밝히고, 그 이유를 설명하는 글이다. 작성자는 이 일을 재미로 하며, 직접 생각하고 직접 탐색하는 과정 자체가 즐겁다고 말한다. 또한 개발과 사이버 보안 분야에서 LLM 사용에 대한 자신의 생각도 함께 정리한다.
items.content_ko: 작성자는 블로그에 쓴 글을 어떤 AI 모델로 조사했느냐는 질문을 자주 받지만, 답은 언제나 자기 머리였다고 말한다. 발표한 리서치에 AI를 쓴 적은 한 번도 없으며, 왜 쓰지 않느냐는 질문에는 '재미'가 가장 큰 이유라고 답한다. 작성자는 코딩하고, 개발자 도구나 Binary Ninja를 몇 시간씩 들여다보고, 라이브러리 소스를 GitHub 코드 검색만으로 추적하는 과정을 즐긴다. 블로그 글은 돈을 벌기 위한 것이 아니며, 수익은 덤일 뿐이라고 밝힌다. 지루한 작업을 AI에 넘기라는 제안에 대해서는, 지루한 부분 중에도 여전히 재미있는 부분이 있고, 무엇보다 LLM이 한 일을 자기 성과로 가져갈 수 없다는 점이 불편하다고 말한다.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Starlink Reportedly Tried to Sell Ukraine a More Expensive Internet Plan After Musk Cut Service
items.content:
Elon Musk reacts after being awarded the National Medal of Science during the "Golden Age of American Innovation Summit" at the Institute of Peace in Washington, D.C., on October 8, 2026. Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation .

After Elon Musk ordered his company SpaceX to throttle Ukraine’s satellite internet service amid disagreements over its military operations earlier this month, the company suggested that Ukraine’s government upgrade its plan to avoid service interruptions, new reporting finds.

The upsell was reported in The Atlantic , which found that SpaceX, which operates Starlink, advised that Ukraine switch to a more expensive plan to avoid service interruptions when asked about the outage.

“If anything can yet restrain Musk from abandoning Ukraine, it may be his own financial interests,” The Atlantic reported this week. “Earlier this month, when U.S. military officials asked SpaceX about the outages in Ukraine, the company advised switching to an upgraded contract to restore Ukraine’s access, U.S. officials told us.”

The incident came just four months after SpaceX’s IPO this June. Reports have suggested that Starlink has already made hundreds of millions of dollars providing Ukraine and its military with internet service since the start of Russia’s invasion.

Early in the war, Musk supposedly “donated” thousands of Starlink satellite kits to the country, making much of Ukraine dependent on the service that holds a relative monopoly over satellite network systems and Ukraine’s ability to conduct critical military operations, such as drone piloting.

The New York Times reported in 2023 that the company is charging $2,500 per terminal per month, with over 42,000 Starlink terminals in use across the country. The co-founder of the Ukraine Defense Fund, which has helped secure Starlink access for the Ukrainian military, told The Atlantic that he estimates there are now over 250,000 Starlink terminals in use across the war zone.

Musk’s capping of service was met with outrage earlier this month , sparking panic within both the Ukrainian and U.S. governments as a large swath of the country’s military was effectively out of service. On Saturday, Musk admitted that he was behind the decision and accused the military of violating Skylink’s terms of service, which Ukraine has denied.

“Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact,” Musk said. “That said, I have nothing but UTTER CONTEMPT for the virtue-signaling evil warmongers who push for endless slaughter and offer no realistic solution to the conflict. May you burn in hell.”

Musk’s seeming turn on Ukraine comes as the Trump administration is increasingly embracing Russia and cutting funding to Ukraine.

The incident has shined a spotlight on Musk’s vast ability to control world events and swing the favor of an entire war toward one side if he so chooses — an enormous amount of power left to one man who represents nothing but his own whims and profits.

Despite this, the Pentagon’s inspector general is effectively refusing to investigate Musk’s interruptions to the service, it told Congress this week.

Critics have already raised concerns about the enormous control that Starlink has over space in low orbit, while its services are the only option in many places that otherwise lack connectivity. Starlink has already faced scrutiny for monopolizing internet services in rural areas of the U.S., and then raising prices dramatically after getting communities hooked.

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

items.title_ko: Starlink, Musk의 우크라이나 서비스 제한 뒤 더 비싼 요금제 권유 보도
items.summary_ko: The Atlantic 보도에 따르면, Elon Musk가 군사 작전을 둘러싼 의견 차이 속에서 SpaceX에 우크라이나 위성 인터넷의 속도를 제한하도록 지시했다. 이후 SpaceX는 서비스 중단을 피하려면 우크라이나 정부가 더 비싼 요금제로 바꿔야 한다고 권했다고 한다. 기사는 Musk의 재정적 이해관계가 우크라이나 지원 중단을 막을 수 있는 유일한 요인일지도 모른다고 지적한다.
items.content_ko: Musk는 이달 초 군사 작전을 둘러싼 의견 차이를 이유로 SpaceX에 우크라이나의 위성 인터넷 서비스를 제한하라고 지시했다. The Atlantic은 이 상황에서 SpaceX가 Starlink 서비스 중단 문제에 대해 우크라이나 정부에 더 비싼 요금제로 업그레이드할 것을 권했다고 보도했다. 미국 군 당국이 우크라이나의 서비스 중단에 대해 SpaceX에 문의했을 때, 회사는 접속을 복구하려면 상위 계약으로 바꾸라고 조언했다고 미국 관계자들이 전했다. The Atlantic은 Musk를 우크라이나 지원에서 물러서지 않게 할 수 있는 것이 있다면 그것은 그의 재정적 이해관계일지도 모른다고 썼다. 이 보도는 Truthout에 함께 실렸다.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

items.summary: 🚨 CVE-2026-84231 📢 Source: apache 💣 CVSS Score: 7.4 (HIGH) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Improper neutralization of input during web page generation in Apache Wicket. org.apache.wicket.markup.html.link
items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-84231 📢 Source: apache 💣 CVSS Score: 7.4 (HIGH) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Improper neutralization of input during web page generation in Apache Wicket. org.apache.wicket.markup.html.link.ExternalLink builds a JavaScript click handler and writes it into the tag's onclick attribute whenever the markup tag the component is bound to is not an a, link or area element. The URL held in the component's model is concatenated into a single-quoted JavaScript string literal in that handler without being escaped for that context. The same happens on the neighbouring branch, taken when popup settings are attached, where the value is concatenated into the window.open() call built by org.apache.wicket.markup.html.link.PopupSettings#getPopupJavaScript(). The only escaping applied is the markup escaping that every attribute value receives as the tag is written, which replaces an apostrophe with a character reference. A browser decodes character references in an attribute value before it compiles the event handler, so the apostrophe is restored, closes the string literal, and the rest of the model value is executed as script in the application's origin. An application is affected where it binds an ExternalLink to a markup tag that is not an anchor, such as a button or a span, and the URL in the model holds data an attacker can influence, which is the ordinary use of the component rather than a misuse of it. Nothing runs until a user activates the element. This issue affects Apache Wicket: from 8.0.0 through 8.19.0. Users of Apache Wicket 7.x or older, which are no longer supported, should upgrade to a supported version. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 8.20.0, which fixes the issue. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-01T22:26:18.525Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-84231

items.content_ko: Apache Wicket의 org.apache.wicket.markup.html.link.ExternalLink는 태그가 a, link, area 요소가 아닐 때 onclick 속성에 들어갈 JavaScript 클릭 핸들러를 만든다. 이때 컴포넌트 모델의 URL 값이 작은따옴표로 감싼 JavaScript 문자열에 이스케이프 없이 이어 붙여진다. 팝업 설정이 있을 때도 PopupSettings#getPopupJavaScript()가 만드는 window.open() 호출에서 같은 문제가 생긴다. 유일한 이스케이프는 태그 작성 시 적용되는 마크업 이스케이프뿐인데, 이는 작은따옴표를 문자 참조로 바꾼다. 브라우저는 이벤트 핸들러를 컴파일하기 전에 속성 값의 문자 참조를 디코딩하므로 작은따옴표가 복원되어 문자열이 닫히고, 나머지 값이 애플리케이션 출처에서 스크립트로 실행된다. 본문이 중간에서 끊겨 있어 영향을 받는 조건은 원문에서 확인해야 한다.

items.title: Memdoor: A team of 5 Qwen3.8-27B models beats Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard
items.content:
Five small models solve a programming problem together: a planner, two

ideators, a solver and a manager, plus a repair worker. Each starts from a

fresh context and talks only through files on disk. A script that runs the

samples decides success, not a model. It is the method of

Memdoor workflow: eight YAML files, no code, no model

The authors' harness rebuilt on the same model, Qwen3.8-27B, with their

prompts, loop and 128K reply cap. The first ten problems of their

LiveCodeBench Hard list, five passes each, graded on every hidden test with

The authors' two columns are the regraded result files in their repository,

the numbers in their paper. Our column is

bench/results/parity-5pass/ : all 50 runs,

each with every request and reply, the program, the grader's output and the

cost. A run took a median of 40 minutes and $0.39; the 50 cost $35.79.

Ten problems, five passes, not the authors' 100. On a sample this small,

9.8 and 9.6 are the same number. The claim is parity with their harness, not

The contests date from spring 2025 and the model may have seen them in

training. Contamination cannot be ruled out, for any column.

Fable 5's column is one call per problem, from the authors' files. It was

The loop sees only the public samples; the score is the hidden tests.

The model ran on OpenRouter, not a local machine.

The one lost problem: the manager invented a wrong counterexample and the

team rewrote a correct program. Twice elsewhere a correct program was

overwritten and then recovered. Both gaps are the authors' loop, kept as is.

The parity check (every request byte for byte against their code), the hosts,

the changes it took and the first run's findings are in NOTES.md .

The same result, on one page: memdoor.ai/docs/team-solve .

curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash

memdoor connect openrouter # or anthropic, openai, gemini, chatgpt

# or no key: memdoor connect local (Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, LM Studio; Ollama needs a 32K window, not its 4K default)

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor

cp -r memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve ~/.memdoor/workflows/

cp -r ../memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve/sample/* . # task.md + tests/1.in … 5.out

memdoor workflow run team-solve --wait # exit 0 when every sample passes

For your own problem, replace task.md and put paired tests/N.in /

tests/N.out beside it. The program is solution.py , read from stdin,

compared to the samples with diff ; it needs Python 3 and bash. /workflow

The steps name no model: whatever /model is pinned to answers, a local one

To change a role, change its prompt in steps/ .

plan ──┬── ideate-a ──┬── solve ── test ── review ── repair ── verify

a proposal each: the most direct provable algorithm, and one from another family

the verdict: a nonzero exit fails the run

Every agent prompt says "fresh context, read the files, do not rely on chat".

The paper credits that ledger discipline for the gain. Each step is one YAML

file in steps/ , in the format of mario ,

the engine underneath; requires: is the DAG.

items.summary_ko: Qwen3.8-27B 모델 5개가 기획자, 아이디어 2개, 해결자, 관리자, 수리 담당으로 역할을 나눠 문제를 푸는 Memdoor 방식을 저자들의 하네스와 같은 모델로 재현했다. LiveCodeBench Hard의 앞 10문제를 각 5회씩 풀었고, 두 결과 수치(9.8과 9.6)는 같은 값으로 볼 만큼 차이가 작다고 밝혔다. 표본이 작고 대회 문제가 학습 데이터에 포함됐을 가능성을 배제할 수 없다고 명시했다.
items.content_ko: 다섯 개의 작은 모델이 역할을 나눠 프로그래밍 문제를 푼다. 기획자, 아이디어 담당 2명, 해결자, 관리자, 수리 담당이 있으며, 각자 새 컨텍스트에서 시작해 디스크의 파일로만 소통한다. 성공 여부는 모델이 아니라 샘플을 실행하는 스크립트가 판정한다. Memdoor 워크플로는 코드 없이 YAML 파일 8개로 구성된다. 저자들의 하네스를 같은 모델(Qwen3.8-27B)과 같은 프롬프트, 루프, 128K 응답 상한으로 재구현했다. LiveCodeBench Hard의 앞 10문제를 각 5회씩 풀고, 모든 숨은 테스트에 대해 채점했다. 비교 대상인 저자 측 수치는 저장소의 재채점 결과 파일이다. 한 번의 실행은 중간값 40분, 비용 $0.39가 들었고, 50회 실행 총비용은 $35.79였다. 10문제 5회 표본은 저자들의 100회보다 훨씬 작아서 결과를 확대 해석할 수 없다고 밝혔다. 주장은 저자 하네스와의 동등성(parity)이다. 대회 문제는 2025년 봄 것이며 모델이 학습 과정에서 봤을 수 있어 오염 가능성을 배제할 수 없다. Fable 5 측 결과는 문제당 한 번의 호출로 얻은 것이라고 한다. 본문이 중간에 끊겨 있다.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED.
